articles.title: Australia planted rubber vine from Madagascar as a garden ornamental in the 1860s; the climbing weed now reaches 30 metres and has covered huge areas of Queensland
articles.summary: Rubber vine began its Australian story as a garden ornamental brought from Madagascar, and it has since become one of the country's most troublesome weeds.
articles.body: Rubber vine began its Australian story as a garden ornamental brought from Madagascar, and it has since become one of the country's most troublesome weeds. Left unchecked, this glossy, trumpet-flowered climber can scramble up to 30 metres into tree canopies, blanket creek lines, smother the native vegetation beneath it, and form dense thickets. It also poisons people and livestock, makes mustering cattle difficult, and reduces food and shelter for native animals. Whether you farm, manage land, garden, or simply care about the bush, knowing how rubber vine spreads, how to recognise it, and what the law requires of you matters.How rubber vine arrived in Australia, from a Madagascan garden to an invasive weedRubber vine is native to southwestern Madagascar, and the New South Wales Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development, through its WeedWise service, notes that it now grows across East Africa, Southeast Asia, the United States, and Central and Southern America. In Australia, its story starts in the 1860s, when it was planted in the gardens of northern Queensland mining towns. By 1917, people were already reporting infestations. During the Second World War, it was grown as a possible source of rubber, which did nothing to slow its movement.From those early plantings, it spread through much of Queensland, the south of Cape York, the Gulf of Carpentaria, the coast as far south as Bundaberg, and west to the Northern Territory border. WeedWise includes a photograph of a Queensland infestation that covered an estimated 700,000 hectares in 1991, which gives a sense of how far one garden plant can travel.How to identify rubber vine, glossy leaves, trumpet-shaped flowers and paired seed podsRubber vine is a perennial, many-stemmed woody shrub or vine. Without support, it grows as an untidy shrub roughly two to three metres tall. Given something to climb, it can reach 30 metres, according to both the New South Wales and Queensland government pages. It produces two kinds of stems. Branched, leafy stems grow up to two metres long, while long, unbranched "whips" of three to eight metres reach out and haul the plant up into nearby vegetation. Stems are smooth and greyish brown, and they ooze a milky sap when broken.The leaves are dark green and glossy, often with a reddish or purplish midrib and stalk. They are oval with a pointed tip, six to ten centimetres long and three to five centimetres wide, and they grow in opposite pairs. The flowers are large, showy and trumpet-shaped, with five light-purple, pink or white petals. Business Queensland, the Queensland Government's business and industry information service, says flowering can occur at any time of year when moisture allows, with only June and July typically flowerless.The seed pods are the most distinctive feature. They are rigid and triangular in cross-section, up to 12 centimetres long, and usually sit in pairs at the end of a short stalk. Each seed carries a tuft of long, silky white hairs. The two agencies give different upper figures for seeds per pod, 450 in Queensland and 840 in New South Wales, but both agree the numbers are large.Several plants can be mistaken for rubber vine. Ornamental rubber vine has smaller, darker pink flowers and fruit shorter than ten centimetres, and it never has purple leaf stalks or midribs. Purple allamanda has leaves in whorls of three or more and rounded fruit. The native bower vine has hairy flowers with a red throat, much smaller pods about six centimetres long, and leaves made up of four to seven leaflets.How rubber vine smothers native forests, riverbank vegetation and pasture across tropical QueenslandRubber vine grows best in semi-arid regions with tropical or subtropical climates, though it needs reliable water. That is why it so often takes hold along creeks, rivers and run-off areas. It tolerates shade and a wide range of temperatures, and only frost knocks back the growth above ground.Business Queensland describes how it smothers riparian vegetation, meaning plants along waterways, and forms dense thickets that spread outward onto hillsides and pasture. The result is lower biodiversity and barriers that impede both stock and native animals. The New South Wales WeedWise page adds that the weed can reduce food and shelter for wildlife and may lower water quality in streams. For graziers, the cost is practical: thick infestations make mustering difficult and take productive land out of use.Why rubber vine spreads so easily and how roots reach 12 metresAccording to WeedWise, a single hectare of rubber vine can produce millions of seeds each year, and about 95 per cent of fresh seed is viable. Most seed stays viable for six to eight months, although in very dry conditions most die within a year. Seeds can survive for more than a month inside floating pods, even in saltwater.Wind carries seeds short distances, while water carries them much further, because the pods float and ride creeks and floods downstream. Seeds can also catch in animal fur or travel in mud and soil on machinery. Business Queensland explains that pods dry and split open about 200 days after forming. Germination still depends on suitable temperature and soil moisture. Below ground, roots can reach 12 metres deep, which is one reason established plants are so hard to remove.Rubber vine is poisonous, dangerous to cattle and people who touch or eat itEvery part of rubber vine is poisonous. WeedWise reports that it contains cardiac glycosides, compounds that affect the heart, brain and gut. Cattle, sheep, goats and horses are all at risk. Grazing animals rarely eat much unless other feed is scarce, but animals have died after eating dry leaves that had fallen to the ground. Cattle that have eaten even a small amount can die of heart failure after vigorous exercise, such as mustering. The most common sign is diarrhoea, often with blood.People are at risk too. The sap irritates skin and can cause burning, rashes and blisters, and dust from dried plants can irritate the throat, nose and eyes. If someone eats any part of the plant and is unconscious, unresponsive or struggling to breathe, call triple zero (000) or go straight to a hospital emergency department. If the person is conscious and responsive, call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 or contact a doctor, and take a piece of the plant for identification.How to control rubber vine: Biological control with rust and mothsBusiness Queensland sets out a layered approach. Fire can control infestations when fuel loads are prepared first, and follow-up treatment is applied. Two successive annual burns are recommended, the first opens up the infestation and kills plants, and the second clears the regrowth. For scattered or medium-density infestations, repeated slashing close to the ground works well. For dense infestations, stickraking or blade ploughing in winter reduces the bulk, after which pasture is sown, windrows are burned, and follow-up work is done.Herbicides can be applied as foliar sprays, basal bark treatments, cut stump treatments or soil applications. Foliar spraying works best on actively growing plants under two metres tall, and not on plants that are water-stressed, yellowing or carrying pods. Cut stump treatment involves cutting within 15 centimetres of the ground and treating the cut surface immediately. Always read the product label and any permit before using a chemical.Two biological control agents are also established: rubber vine rust, a fungal disease, and a leaf-feeding moth. Both cause defoliation that appears to reduce seed production, but they do not usually kill established plants. Their effect depends on how abundant they are.In New South Wales, the advice is different. WeedWise asks people not to treat or dispose of rubber vine themselves. Report it, and the department's Agriculture and Biosecurity team will lead the response.Rubber vine laws in Queensland and New South Wales: What you must and must not do as a landholderIn Queensland, rubber vine is a category 3 restricted invasive plant under the Biosecurity Act 2014. You must not give it away, sell it or release it into the environment, and you must take all reasonable and practical steps to minimise the biosecurity risk it poses. Local governments also maintain biosecurity plans for invasive plants, and some of the actions in them may be required under local laws.In New South Wales, rubber vine is a prohibited matter under the Biosecurity Act 2015. Dealing with it is an offence; it must not be sold anywhere in the state, and anyone who sees or suspects it must notify the Department of Primary Industries immediately. WeedWise reports that rubber vine has been found at several properties in the north west of the state, mostly around homesteads and sheds, and that those sites are under an eradication program. If you spot a plant that looks like rubber vine in New South Wales, call the Biosecurity Helpline on 1800 680 244. articles.title: Man dies after entering tiger enclosure at England wildlife park
articles.summary: Emergency services called to the scene after reports of a man entering the tiger enclosure at a UK wildlife park.
articles.body:
A man has died after entering a tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England and being attacked by one of the animals, police said.

South Yorkshire Police said officers and emergency medical staff were called to Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster at about 1:35pm on Saturday (12:35 GMT) after receiving reports that a man had entered the enclosure.

He died at the scene. It was not immediately clear how he got in.

The tiger was not injured and stayed inside the enclosure during the incident, police said, adding that there was no wider risk to the public.

The park was evacuated, and officers remained at the scene on Saturday night.

“The man’s family is aware and is being supported by specialist officers. Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time,” police said in a statement.

Police also confirmed they were aware of footage circulating on social media that appeared to show the man inside the enclosure shortly before the attack, urging members of the public not to share the distressing video.

The park said it had closed after a serious incident involving the tiger enclosure and would remain closed until Sunday.

“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,” the park said in a statement on its website.

“The safety and wellbeing of our visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority”.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operating in 2009, and its Land of the Tigers attraction – a purpose-built 0.4-hectare (2-acre) reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers – opened in 2011.

A raised walkway, 300 metres (985 feet) long, lets visitors watch the tigers roam through woodland and grassland and play in a waterfall pool, the park said.

articles.title: World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport
articles.summary: Trump condemns ‘terrible’ attack and says the US is evaluating whether to join Saudi Arabia’s attacks on the Houthis.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia has accused Yemen’s Houthis of killing at least 12 people and wounding 300 others in a third attack on the Riyadh international airport this week.

The victims on Saturday included four Saudis, two people from ⁠Bangladesh and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

The attack was the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.

It came as the war in Yemen intensifies, with the Houthis battling forces aligned with the internationally recognised government for control of the country. Saudi Arabia is waging an air campaign against the Houthis to support the ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.

US President Donald Trump described the attack as “terrible” and said he “will be speaking” with Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, soon. He also said he was evaluating whether the US should join the war against the Houthis.

“We may. We’re gonna look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We’ll move very quickly,” he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said the Houthi attack killed an American and called for an end to “these reprehensible attacks”.

“We stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families,” he wrote on X.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres issued a statement on X, saying he is “deeply shocked” and strongly condemns “Saturday’s lethal attack by the Houthis on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh”.

He said that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violated international law and “must cease immediately”.

Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, said the deadly strikes on civilian airports in Saudi Arabia represent “a grave escalation”.

“Such actions pose a serious threat to regional security, perpetuate cycles of violence and complicate even more peace efforts for Yemen,” he said in a statement.

The Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed its “strong condemnation” of the Houthi attacks, denouncing their “flagrant violation” of international law, and the “disregard” for the safety of citizens that they entail.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Houthi attacks, describing them as a “serious violation of Saudi sovereignty and a direct threat to the security of the region, the safety of civilians, civil facilities and air navigation”.

It expressed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said Doha supported “all legitimate measures” the kingdom “takes to preserve its sovereignty, security and safety of its territories”.

Pakistan also strongly condemned the attack, calling it a “heinous act of terrorism” and a “grave threat to regional peace and security”.

The Pakistani Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Islamabad – which has recently activated a mutual defence pact with Riyadh over the attacks – “stands in unwavering solidarity” with Saudi Arabia.

Jordan’s King Abdullah offered condolences to Saudi Arabia’s King Salman and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman over the attacks and expressed his kingdom’s full solidarity with Riyadh.

The country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the “brutal aggression” by the Houthis, describing it as a “dangerous escalation” and a “blatant breach of international law”.

The sultanate also denounced the attack and emphasised the “necessity of prioritising the voice of wisdom and self-restraint, and avoiding actions that would expand the scope of escalation, in order to preserve the security and stability of the region”.

The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared “its full solidarity with the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia” and said it supported “all measures taken by the Kingdom to safeguard its security, sovereignty, and the safety of its citizens and residents”.

Japan’s embassy in Saudi Arabia strongly condemned the repeated attacks by the Houthis, saying assaults on civilians “cannot be tolerated” under any circumstances.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney described the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, particularly the strike on King Khalid International airport in Riyadh, as “abhorrent”.

“There can be no justification for attacks on civilian infrastructure,” he wrote on X, adding that Canada “condemns these reckless acts of violence in the strongest possible terms”.

articles.title: Sanjeev Kapoor’s Chilli Garlic Potato Shots are the perfect homemade alternative to frozen snacks
articles.summary: Midnight cravings have a rather inconvenient habit of showing up when you have the least energy to cook.
articles.body: Midnight cravings have a rather inconvenient habit of showing up when you have the least energy to cook. You could be halfway through a presentation, three episodes deep into a series you promised yourself you would watch just one episode of, or hosting friends who have somehow finished an entire bowl of snacks before the main course has even arrived. The solution? Finger food that requires little effort but delivers on flavour.But before you reach for another packet of frozen potato bites, celebrity chef Sanjeev Kapoor has a recipe worth trying. His Chilli Garlic Potato Shots bring together the familiar comfort of potatoes, the heat of green chillies and the unmistakable punch of garlic in small crispy bites. They are easy to prepare, need only a handful of everyday ingredients and can be served at everything: from children's birthday parties to impromptu movie nights.And unlike the frozen snacks you buy by the packet, these are made fresh in your kitchen, with the seasoning and ingredients firmly in your control.Why settle for frozen snacks when you can make your ownFrozen snacks have earned their place in Indian kitchens for a reason. They are convenient, require minimal preparation and can be cooked straight from the freezer. However, convenience does not always translate into the best eating experience.Depending on the product, frozen potato snacks may contain added starches, salt, flavourings and other ingredients to maintain their texture and taste. Some commercially prepared varieties are also pre-fried, meaning that the final preparation can involve additional oil. Deep-frying them at home can make it difficult to control how much oil ends up in the finished snack.If you want a snack with a straightforward ingredient list and a flavour profile you can adjust to your liking, homemade potato shots are a practical alternative. Sanjeev Kapoor's recipe uses boiled potatoes, garlic paste, chillies, herbs and cornflour to create a mixture that can be shaped, fried and served fresh. You can increase the chilli for adults, keep the heat mild for children or experiment with the seasoning depending on what you have in your pantry.What makes Sanjeev Kapoor's Chilli Garlic Potato Shots special?Potatoes are a dependable starting point for snacks because their soft, starchy texture makes them easy to shape. Once boiled and grated, they form the base of this recipe, while cornflour helps bind the mixture and gives the shots structure.The flavour, however, comes from the combination of garlic and chillies. Garlic paste brings a savoury intensity, red chilli flakes provide a lingering warmth, and chopped green chillies add a sharper kick. Dried mixed herbs and crushed black peppercorns round out the seasoning without requiring an elaborate spice mix.The contrast in textures is what makes these bites particularly appealing. The outside turns golden and crisp during frying, while the inside remains soft and packed with flavour. Served straight from the kadai with tomato ketchup, they are the sort of snack that can easily disappear before everyone has had a chance to take their first bite.How to make Chilli Garlic Potato Shots at homeIngredients2 large potatoes, boiled and peeled1 tbsp garlic paste2 green chillies, finely chopped½ tsp red chilli flakes½ tsp dried mixed herbsCrushed black peppercorns, to taste2–3 tbsp cornflour, plus extra for dustingSalt, to tasteOil, for deep-fryingTomato ketchup, for servingMethodGrate the boiled and peeled potatoes into a bowl. Add the garlic paste, chopped green chillies, red chilli flakes, dried mixed herbs, crushed black peppercorns, cornflour and salt. Mix until the ingredients are evenly combined. Lightly dust a clean work surface with cornflour. Roll the potato mixture into a slender log, adding a little more cornflour, if necessary, to help it hold its shape. Cut the log into small, bite-sized pieces. Heat sufficient oil in a kadai over medium heat. To check whether it is ready, add a tiny piece of the mixture: it should sizzle steadily without browning immediately. Carefully add the potato shots in small batches. Fry until they are golden brown and crisp on the outside, turning them as needed for even cooking. Avoid overcrowding the kadai, as this can lower the oil temperature and leave the shots greasy. Remove the shots with a slotted spoon and drain on absorbent paper. Serve immediately with tomato ketchup.Can you air-fry them instead?If deep-frying is not your preferred cooking method, these potato shots can also be adapted for an air fryer. Shape the mixture as instructed, lightly brush or spray the pieces with oil and arrange them in a single layer in the basket. Air-fry at around 190°C, checking after 10 minutes and turning them as needed until the outside is crisp and golden. The exact cooking time will depend on the size of the shots and your appliance.Keep in mind that the texture may differ from deep-fried potato shots. Since the mixture is soft, chilling the shaped pieces for 15–20 minutes before cooking can help them hold together. If the mixture feels too wet, add cornflour gradually rather than adding too much at once.You can also prepare the potato mixture in advance and refrigerate it in a covered container. Shape the shots shortly before cooking for a convenient snack when guests arrive.The snack that deserves a permanent place on your menuServe these Chilli Garlic Potato Shots when your children's friends come over, bring them out during a cricket match, or arrange them on a platter when you are hosting a party and need something to keep everyone occupied before dinner. They are equally suited to those evenings when the only company you have is a television screen and an inexplicable craving for something crunchy.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: Four people have died and hundreds of thousands have been left without electricity after Hurricane Isaias battered parts of the southern United States
articles.body: Four people have died and hundreds of thousands have been left without electricity after Hurricane Isaias battered parts of the southern United States with powerful winds and heavy rain. The storm damaged buildings, uprooted trees and raised fears of flash floods and tornadoes across the Southeast.Officials reported two deaths each in Florida and Alabama. An estimated 500,000 people across several states were without power by Saturday evening, according to outage tracker PowerOutage.Nearly 900,000 customers had lost electricity in the initial hours after the storm made landfall, according to BBC reports.Isaias struck Florida’s Gulf Coast late Friday with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (168 km/h) before weakening into a post-tropical cyclone. Although the storm weakened overnight, officials warned that heavy rain and flooding remained a threat.Trees fall on homes, buildings damagedIn Florida’s Escambia County, a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home, while a man died from carbon monoxide poisoning after a generator was operated in his garage, Sheriff Chip Simmons said.Four members of the man’s family, aged between four and 72, were treated and were expected to survive, the Associated Press reported.In Alabama, one person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, Fire Chief Cory Moon said. A second storm-related death was reported in Barbour County after a motor vehicle crash involving a fallen tree, according to Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency.The storm also caused scattered damage along Florida’s Gulf Coast. Hurricane-force winds blew the roof off a hotel in Pensacola, while the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage”. In Destin, a boathouse was flattened, and part of a high-rise building’s facade was torn away in Panama City Beach.Isaias also ripped rooftops and facades from hotels and condominiums along the Florida Panhandle. Authorities in Mobile, Alabama, reported numerous fallen trees and power lines.Emergency declarations, flood warningsAlabama, Florida and Georgia declared states of emergency ahead of the storm, while Florida and Alabama issued mandatory evacuation orders for thousands of residents.US President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Georgia after earlier approving similar measures for Florida and Alabama, allowing federal assistance to be provided.The US Department of Energy also authorised emergency exchanges of crude oil from the nation’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address potential supply disruptions caused by the storm.The National Weather Service warned that parts of Georgia and the Carolinas could experience heavy rainfall capable of triggering flash floods.Isaias was expected to move into the Tennessee Valley before reaching the mid-Atlantic region on Sunday. Forecasters also warned that flooding could extend into the Appalachian region.Despite warnings of storm surges, several major coastal routes were open by daybreak on Saturday and had avoided the widespread damage to trees and power lines often seen after major hurricanes.Meanwhile, in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Simon strengthened into a Category 4 storm as it approached Mexico’s coast. It was expected to bring heavy rainfall from Sunday to parts of southwestern Mexico, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.Tropical Storm Rachel was also forecast to bring strong winds and heavy rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.You use AI every day. articles.title: US forces disable ship ‘attempting to run’ Iran blockade in Gulf of Oman
articles.summary: US military jet strikes stern of commercial cargo ship ‘without harming the crew’, CENTCOM says.
articles.body:
United States forces have disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after its crew “ignored repeated warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran”, according to Central Command (CENTCOM).

A US military fighter jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica, also known as the Arika Sun, with a precision munition on Saturday, “fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the crew”, CENTCOM said in a statement. The vessel was attempting to transit regional waters after “having previously departed an Iranian port”.

CENTCOM said its forces resumed their blockade against all ships “entering or departing Iranian ports on July 14”, disabling four commercial vessels and turning around 135 ships during “three months of strict enforcement”.

US forces also destroyed 10 tankers linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) “multibillion-dollar shadow network” over the same period, CENTCOM said.

US Senator Chris Murphy questioned the military strike, writing on X: “What is this all for? Why are taxpayers paying billions to hit commercial ships?”

“Apparently the goal is to gain leverage in order to convince the Iranians to let us pay them billions to return everything to the way it all was before the war,” the Democratic politician added. “What a disaster.”

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency acknowledged the incident on Sunday, saying that it had received “a report of an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman” and that authorities were investigating.

Meanwhile, the IRGC said it struck a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz for attempting to take an “illegal route”, as Tehran seeks to enforce its own blockade on the vital waterway.

In a statement carried by official Iranian media, the IRGC claimed Iranian forces “have taken control of the administration of the strait”.

“In carrying out this mission, a few hours ago, a giant LPG carrier named NV Sunshine, owned by NatWit, which was attempting to transit via the illegal route south of the Strait of Hormuz, was struck,” the statement said.

The UKMTO said on Sunday that an outbound tanker in the strait was struck on the port side by an unknown projectile, causing a fire on board. The UK agency said crew members were reported safe, while the damage and environmental impact remained unknown at the time of the report.

Tehran has attempted to enforce control over the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war on Iran, insisting that ships obtain permission to cross via its preferred routes. However, vessels have increasingly risked taking an alternative route hugging the strait’s southern coast.

The UK maritime agency said on Thursday that a vessel sailing 94km (58 miles) north of Madinat ash Shamal, off the north coast of Qatar, was struck by multiple projectiles, resulting in several casualties.

The agency did not specify the origin of the ship or the number of people killed or injured, adding that authorities were investigating the incident amid a recent rise in attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz.

Ships in the Gulf attempting to cross the strait, which is the sole maritime route in or out of the oil-rich region, have faced repeated attacks since the US and Israel began the war in late February.

The Strait of Hormuz remains vital to the global economy, with about a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passing through the passage before the war began.

articles.body: US President Donald Trump joked about renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean as “Trump Ocean” or “Ocean of the Americas” during a campaign rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, on Saturday.Referring to the earlier renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, Trump said the United States needed an ocean and a major river to rename.“So we’ve got the Gulf, we’ve got a beautiful lake,” Trump said. “So we need a river, we need an ocean, so I was thinking of either the Atlantic or the Pacific, we'd call it Trump Ocean or Ocean of the Americas, something like that.”Last year, Trump signed an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. articles.title: Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government
articles.summary: Medical services in Taiz risk shutting down as fuel, medicines, and supplies run alarmingly low under Houthi blockade.
articles.body:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has warned of an “imminent health and humanitarian catastrophe” in the besieged city of Taiz, in the country’s southwest, as the Houthis continue their siege and “obstruct essential supplies”.

Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population said in a statement on Saturday that medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and fuel at the city’s health facilities were “nearing depletion”.

It said emergency care, surgery, intensive care, dialysis and neonatal services could be forced to stop if the situation continued, putting patients, injured people, pregnant women and newborns “at immediate risk”.

Fuel shortages also threaten electricity generators, ambulances and the cold chains that keep medicines and vaccines usable, which could cause “severe complications and preventable deaths”, the ministry said.

It demanded the siege be lifted immediately, and supply routes reopened, with safe passage for patients, ambulances, health workers and aid.

It called on the United Nations and humanitarian organisations to “deliver medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies, oxygen and fuel” to the city’s health facilities.

“Every delay increases the risk of service interruption and loss of life,” the ministry said.

The Houthis, an armed group backed by Iran and also known as Ansar Allah, seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government. They control the country’s north and northeast.

Taiz endured a devastating Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, when Yemeni government forces were confined to an enclave in the city centre.

The siege was broken in 2016, though the Houthis kept a partial blockade through other access points. In 2024, they agreed to reopen a route from the east, but it has been closed after fighting resumed.

The renewed siege took shape in early October.

The Houthis launched an offensive along the Red Sea coast of the Taiz governorate in September, capturing the port city of Mocha, and by October 4 had taken the town of At Turbah, cutting the last main road between Taiz city and other government-held areas.

Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, began a counteroffensive in early October.

Nabil Jamil, director-general of the Yemeni government’s planning and development office in the Taiz governorate, told Al Jazeera the current siege is “more comprehensive and its impact more severe than in 2015”.

He said about 2.8 million people live in government-held areas of the governorate, along with 200,000 who have recently been displaced.

Fuel has become scarce, and on the black market, the price of a 20-litre (5.2-gallon) container of petrol has risen from 30,000 Yemeni riyals ($19) to 90,000 ($58).

“We are still waiting for a response or intervention on the ground,” Jamil said.

The UN refugee agency and the World Health Organization have warned that the fighting is putting Yemen’s fragile health system in peril.

“Civilians must never be turned into a means of exerting pressure in any conflict,” said Nabil Sharyan, a lawyer and head of the Justice for Rights and Development Organization.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) MP Manoj Jha has approached the Supreme Court challenging the Delhi Police’s handling of protests held in the national capital on October 10 against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Election Commission.The plea alleges disproportionate use of force, illegal detentions and house arrests of protesters, including student leaders, advocates, politicians and civilians.It also raises allegations of sexual harassment of women protesters and claims that the police failed to act against individuals who allegedly assaulted demonstrators, according to Live Law report.Plea alleges mass detentions, disruption of public servicesJha has claimed that more than 6,000 people, including former chief ministers, MPs, senior advocates, lawyers, students and civilians unconnected with the protests, were detained by the authorities.The petition states that 250 trains were reportedly cancelled ahead of the demonstrations and 45 Metro stations in Delhi were closed on October 10. Portable mobile phone jammers were reportedly installed as well, despite the absence of any statutory authority empowering Delhi Police to jam telecommunications, the petition claims.Jha has sought a declaration that the police action between October 9 and 10, including detentions, internet suspension, restrictions on Metro and train services, and the alleged disproportionate use of force, was illegal.Petition raises allegations of harassment of women protestersThe plea further cites reports of uniformed personnel removing their name tags, unidentified men in plain clothes and self-proclaimed vigilantes allegedly being present during the protests.It also alleges sexual molestation and groping of women protesters, claiming that such incidents violated the principles laid down in Anita Thakur v. articles.title: Adventurer who lost a leg is impersonated by online fraudsters
articles.summary: Luke Tarrant says he is "disgusted" that fraudsters are pretending to be him on social media.
articles.body:
An adventurer who lost a leg in a motorbike crash has warned people not to send money in response to social media messages from someone pretending to be him.

Luke Tarrant, 30, from Bedford, who has more than 770,000 followers on TikTok and Instagram, said he was "disgusted" and extremely angry after discovering someone had being scammed into transferring their life savings to a fake Facebook page.

He said the page had been created in his name with private messages asking if people had "anything you can spare" as "things have been a bit difficult lately".

Tarrant said he reported it to Meta, which owns the site. The company confirmed the page had been removed "for violating our policies".

Tarrant posted his annoyance on his Instagram page to warn people that others had been stealing his videos and posting them on fake accounts.

He said: "If you're speaking to me on Facebook, stop right now, do not send any money."

He said he is bad at responding to direct messages and had been alerted to the issue by his girlfriend and his gym.

They told him a woman had transferred her life savings to someone she thought was him and was left totally embarrassed.

He said money was raised for him by his gym in 2024 when he lost his leg while travelling through South America , but the fundraiser was quickly taken down when he didn't need any more money.

The only other time he has asked for money was when he fundraised for care, support and specialist equipment for gold medal Paralympian, David Smith who has terminal cancer.

He said as his following has grown on social media, so have the fake accounts pretending to be him.

"I keep reporting them, they get taken down but it seems to take forever, it should be easier to get them taken down."

Tarrant said he was also aware of AI being used to impersonate his voice in messages and videos and it was "scary".

He said: "If you are ever asked for money online or are chatting to someone with a public profile, have a second thought.

"This is the new way that's smarter at impersonating people, we all need a new level of awareness we didn't need before. Please be careful."

A spokesperson for Meta said: "Scammers are relentless and continuously evolve their tactics to try to evade detection, which is why we're constantly developing new ways to make it harder for scammers to deceive others.

"Last year alone we took down more than 159 million scam ads with over 92% detected proactively before anyone reported them.

"We also removed 10.9 million accounts associated with criminal scam centres.

"We've built additional detection models, specifically for celeb-bait, that automatically incorporate what we have learned about the changing tactics used in ads to help us improve."

A spokesperson for Bedfordshire Police advised people to be vigilant when approached by online accounts alleging to be public figures or friends.

They said: "Scammers can easily create convincing false profiles, which are built to use trusted relationships to manipulate people into sending money, bank details or vouchers."

The spokesperson advised people to read the force's online safety guides .

Report Fraud said if anyone is asked for money by someone they have recently started speaking with online, it should be warning sign.

The organisation said anyone who believes they have been a victim should report it online or call 0300 123 2040.

articles.title: Peterborough's literacy rates improve in year of reading
articles.summary: Children in Peterborough are encouraged to choose their own reading material
articles.body:
A Peterborough headteacher says allowing children to choose what they want to read is an important part of improving literacy rates.

St Augustine's Junior School have been promoting a love of reading in their children, with lessons including making book covers, writing graffiti walls and recording book reviews on tablet devices.

In 2026, 77% of children at St Augustine's achieved the expected reading rate, above the national average of 75%.

2026 is the National Year of Reading, an initiative set up by the Department for Education and the National Literacy Trust to improve reading rates.

'We encourage everyone to read what interests them'

"The traditional way of every child sitting down with the same reading book might be a little bit old school now" says Sam Brunt.

"We encourage everyone to read what interests them, whether that's a recipe book, whether that's a non-fiction book or a traditional story novel, anything that gets them interested."

Those comments are echoed by year six class teacher Stefano Rocchio: "Reading is kind of the backbone of what we do in school, without reading they are going to struggle with a lot of the other aspects of the curriculum.

"We try and incorporate reading into everything that we do in school, promoting it through reading cafes, activities and weekly reading sessions."

The children say they enjoy choosing which books to read and show lots of diverse tastes.

Isha picked out 'The Boy in the Dress' and says: "It's funny and sad. It's like a comic and you have lots of laughs. This was my first ever thick book I read."

Annesha enjoys reading a book about artist Frida Kahlo, from the children's biography series 'Little People, Big Dreams.' She says it's because she 'likes art and the pictures.'

Zina is challenging herself with a longer mystery book called 'Tunnels.'

"I really like murder mystery books which sometimes make me cry, this one made me cry a bit when I first read it."

Leja is reading a Horrible Histories book called 'The Woeful Second World War.'

"It's very interesting and gives lots of facts about the Second World War."

The National Literacy Trust has been working with the Department of Education to run 'The National Year of Reading' in 2026.

They have been working in cities like Peterborough, where they run activities to promote reading, including working with Peterborough United .

That work has been supported by Peterborough City Council. Katy Cole, the Labour cabinet member for children and young people, says it has been a great help across some of the city's deprived wards.

"In areas where they have been focusing their efforts we have seen a real improvement in the love, the joy, the enthusiasm and the engagement with reading."

However, the council has faced financial pressures recently, and they consulted on closing a number of their smaller local libraries around the city.

They included Woodston library, which is a short walk from St Augustine's school and facilitates regular visits from the pupils.

Jennie Storey, the Chair of the Friends of Woodston Library says libraries are 'a magical place' and the children are always 'smiling, laughing and reading' when they visit.

The importance of reading for young children is often best summed up by parents.

Katie Rose has had her first children's book published called 'The Monster Story'.

She made up the story for her four year old daughter when she was waiting for an operation. She says it's really important that parents get involved in reading too:

"It's just that time together, you sit there together and you pick up a book and you cuddle. It's one of our favourite times of the day."
